title: Modern CPU Microarchitecture
summary: How a real core — front-end, back-end, uops, and all — ties every earlier topic into one machine.

blocks.markdown:
A modern core is two halves working together: a **front-end** that fetches and decodes instructions, and a **back-end** that executes them out of order and retires results in order.

- Everything from [pipelining](pipelining) and [branch-prediction](branch-prediction) lives inside the front-end.
- Everything from [instruction-level-parallelism](instruction-level-parallelism) lives inside the back-end.
- This topic is the capstone: same pieces, assembled into one real chip.

blocks.subTitle: The two halves
blocks.markdown:
What each half owns.

| Half | Job |
|---|---|
| Front-end | Fetch, decode, predict branches |
| Back-end | Schedule, execute, retire |

The front-end feeds work in program order; the back-end runs it in any order it can.

The **front-end** pulls instructions from the [instruction-set-architecture](instruction-set-architecture) stream and turns them into work the back-end understands.

- **Fetch** reads raw instruction bytes using the predicted path from a branch predictor.
- **Decode** figures out what each instruction means and breaks it into smaller pieces.
- For a CISC ISA like x86, one instruction often decodes into several simpler operations.

A **micro-op (uop)** is a simple, fixed-shape internal instruction — one register read, one ALU op, one memory access.

- Decode breaks each CISC instruction into one or more RISC-like uops.
- A simple `add` may be one uop; a complex `push` may be several.
- Uops give the back-end a uniform shape to schedule, rename, and execute — regardless of how messy the original ISA is.

Decoding CISC instructions is slow and power-hungry, so cores cache the result.

- The **uop cache** stores already-decoded uops for recently-run instruction addresses.
- On a hit, the front-end skips fetch and decode entirely and feeds uops straight in — faster and cheaper.
- Hot loops (tight code run millions of times) live almost entirely out of the uop cache.

The uop stream crosses from front-end to back-end through a queue, then fans out for out-of-order work.

Boxes in order: 'Fetch', 'Decode', 'Uop Queue', then a dashed divider, then 'Out-of-Order Back-End (Schedulers, Execution Ports)', then 'Retire'. One arrow flowing left to right, label under the divider 'front-end -> back-end'. 2-3 word box labels only. >>>

Everything left of the divider runs in order; everything right of it can run out of order.

Before scheduling, each uop's registers are **renamed**: mapped from the small set of architectural registers (the ones the ISA names) onto a much larger pool of physical registers.

- Renaming removes false dependencies where two instructions reuse the same register name for unrelated values.
- A real core keeps hundreds of physical registers — far more than the ISA exposes — precisely to make this work.
- This is what lets independent instructions run in parallel instead of waiting on a reused name.

After renaming, each uop waits in a **reservation station** — a small buffer that holds uops until their inputs are ready.

- A uop "wakes up" and issues to an execution port the moment its operands arrive, not in program order.
- This is the core mechanism behind [instruction-level-parallelism](instruction-level-parallelism): many uops can be in flight, waiting or running, at once.
- Full reservation stations stall new uops from issuing, capping how much overlap is possible.

Uops finish out of order, but the ISA promises results appear in program order. The **reorder buffer (ROB)** fixes that.

- Every uop gets a ROB entry in program order when it's dispatched.
- It executes whenever ready, but only **retires** — commits its result permanently — once every older ROB entry has retired.
- The ROB is also what lets the core recover cleanly from a mispredicted branch or a fault: just discard everything after the bad entry.

The back-end doesn't have one ALU — it has several **execution ports**, each wired to specific units (integer ALU, floating point, load, store).

- Multiple ready uops can issue to different ports in the same cycle.
- A wide core might issue 6-8 uops per cycle across all ports combined.
- Real programs rarely fill every port every cycle — dependencies and limited ILP leave some ports idle most of the time.

Memory uops get their own out-of-order machinery, because address checks make them trickier than ALU ops.

- The **load queue** and **store queue** track in-flight reads and writes so the core can check for conflicts (a load reading an address an older store hasn't written yet).
- **Store-to-load forwarding** lets a load grab data straight from a pending store instead of waiting for memory.
- Getting this wrong breaks correctness, so these queues are heavily guarded logic.

Every memory access needs an address translation and a cache lookup, both multi-level for speed.

- A small **L1 TLB** (translation lookaside buffer, caches virtual-to-physical address mappings) is checked first; a larger **L2 TLB** backs it up before falling to a full page-table walk.
- Data flows through [cache-fundamentals](cache-fundamentals)'s L1, L2, and shared L3 caches, each bigger and slower than the last.
- A miss at every level — TLB and cache — is what turns a 4-cycle load into one costing hundreds.

**Simultaneous multithreading (SMT)**, e.g. Intel's Hyper-Threading, runs two threads on one physical core at once.

- Both threads share the same front-end, reservation stations, ports, and caches — but each keeps its own architectural registers.
- When one thread stalls (say, on a cache miss), the other's uops fill the idle ports instead of wasting the cycle.
- Gains are modest — often 20-30%, not 2x — because the threads compete for the same shared resources.

**IPC** (instructions retired per cycle) grew fast for decades, then flattened.

- Real code has limited natural ILP — most programs simply don't have enough independent instructions to fill a wider core.
- Bigger reservation stations, more ports, and deeper ROBs all hit diminishing returns and rising power cost.
- That's why gains now come from more cores, SMT, and specialized units — not just a wider single pipeline. See [power-performance-scaling](power-performance-scaling).

Common mistakes:

- **"Out-of-order execution means results can appear out of order."** No — the ROB always retires in program order; only internal execution is reordered.
- **"More execution ports always help."** Only if the code has enough ILP to use them; otherwise ports sit idle.
- **"SMT doubles a core's throughput."** It shares one core's resources between threads — a modest boost, not a second core.

blocks.subTitle: What are micro-ops
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What are micro-ops, and why decode into them?**

Micro-ops (uops) are simple, fixed-shape internal instructions that a complex CISC instruction gets broken into during decode. The back-end only ever has to schedule, rename, and execute one uniform shape, regardless of how irregular the original ISA is — that uniformity is what makes wide out-of-order execution practical.

blocks.subTitle: Front-end vs back-end
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What's the difference between a core's front-end and back-end?**

The front-end fetches and decodes instructions in program order, predicting branches to stay ahead. The back-end takes the resulting uops, renames their registers, executes them out of order across multiple ports, and retires results in order through the reorder buffer. Front-end feeds; back-end does the actual work.

blocks.subTitle: Extracting ILP
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How does a modern CPU extract instruction-level parallelism from serial code?**

It renames registers to kill false dependencies, holds uops in reservation stations until their real inputs are ready, and issues each one the moment it can run — regardless of program order. Multiple execution ports let several ready uops run in the same cycle. The reorder buffer then makes all of this look sequential from the outside.

blocks.subTitle: What the ROB is for
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is the reorder buffer for?**

It restores program order on top of out-of-order execution. Every uop gets a ROB entry when dispatched and only retires — commits its result — once all older entries have retired, even if it finished first. It also gives the core a clean recovery point: on a branch misprediction or fault, everything after the bad entry is simply discarded.

blocks.subTitle: Why IPC growth slowed
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why have single-core IPC gains slowed down?**

Real programs have limited natural ILP, so widening a core past a point just leaves extra ports and buffers idle. Bigger reservation stations and deeper reorder buffers also cost rising power and die area for shrinking returns. That's pushed the industry toward more cores, SMT, and specialized accelerators instead of ever-wider single pipelines.
